hints: Think about how many product molecules form when propene reacts with HBr, and what happens to the C=C bond.
walkthrough:
Picture what addition means**
Think of the word add as joining together. You start with propene, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$, and $\text{HBr}$. You finish with just one molecule, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{Br}$. Nothing is lost, no small molecule like water is thrown out. Everything joins into one.
Final answer: Two or more reactants combine to form only one single product.

hints: Remember that the C=C pi bond is electron rich and HBr is polar, so decide which atom of HBr is electron poor and will be attacked first.
Recall where curly arrows must start from, either a bond or a lone pair, and where they must point to in the first step of electrophilic addition.
Think about which carbon of propene gets the H so that the positive charge ends up on the more substituted carbon to make 2-bromopropane.
Consider what nucleophile is left after the first step and how its lone pair forms the second bond to the carbocation.
walkthrough:
Spot the electron rich and electron poor sites**
The $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond in propene has a pi electron cloud above and below the bond. It is a great electron donor. In $\text{H}-\text{Br}$, Br is more electronegative than H, so you must show $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. The $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ is the electrophile.

Draw the first attack to make the carbocation**
Draw a curly arrow starting from the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond and pointing to the $\text{H}^{\delta+}$. At the same time draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{H}-\text{Br}$ bond onto Br. The H adds to the end $\text{CH}_2$ carbon, the bond breaks heterolytically, and you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$ plus $\text{Br}^{-}$ with three lone pairs and a negative charge.

Check the intermediate**
For 2-bromopropane the intermediate must be the secondary carbocation, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$, with the positive charge on the central carbon. Show the charge clearly on carbon. This is the carbon that Br will later join.

Finish with bromide attack**
Now $\text{Br}^{-}$ acts as a nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ directly to the $\text{C}^{+}$ of the intermediate. This forms the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond and gives $\text{H}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{Br}$, which is 2-bromopropane.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C}=\text{C}$ pi bond attacks $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$; curly arrow from $\text{C}=\text{C}$ to H, curly arrow from $\text{H}-\text{Br}$ bond to Br to give $\text{Br}^{-}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$ intermediate. Step 2: lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ attacks $\text{C}^{+}$; curly arrow from $\text{Br}^{-}$ lone pair to $\text{C}^{+}$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$.

hints: Compare the two possible carbocation intermediates that could form when H adds to either end of the C=C bond.
Recall how alkyl groups push electron density toward a positive carbon and how the number of attached alkyl groups affects stability.
walkthrough:
Compare the two routes**
If H adds to the terminal $\text{CH}_2$, you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$, a secondary carbocation. If H adds to the central carbon, you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^{+}$, a primary carbocation. Both are possible in theory, but they are not equally stable.

Link alkyl groups to stability**
Alkyl groups push electron density toward the $\text{C}^{+}$ by the positive inductive effect. This spreads out the positive charge and lowers energy. The secondary cation has two methyl groups feeding electrons to $\text{C}^{+}$, while the primary cation has only one ethyl group. More electron donation means more stable, so the secondary route dominates and 2-bromopropane is the major product.

Final answer: 2-bromopropane forms via the more stable secondary carbocation intermediate.
This is stabilised by the greater positive inductive effect of two methyl groups attached to $\text{C}^{+}$, compared to one ethyl group in the primary carbocation leading to 1-bromopropane.

hints: Look at the final concentration of X in Fig. 3.2 after 400 s and ask whether X has been completely used up.
walkthrough:
Read the end of the curve**
In Fig. 3.2 the concentration of X starts at $1.0 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and falls, but after about 400 s it becomes flat at a value above zero. That flat line means the reaction has stopped while X is still present. If X were limiting it would reach zero. Since X is left over, $\text{H}_2$ must have run out first, so $\text{H}_2$ limits the reaction.
Final answer: $\text{H}_2$ is the limiting reagent because some alkene X remains at the end, concentration of X levels off at about $0.12 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and does not fall to zero.

hints: Recall that gradient of a concentration time graph equals rate, then observe whether the curve gets steeper or flatter with time.
walkthrough:
Link steepness to speed**
Gradient means how steep the curve is, and for concentration against time, gradient = rate. At the start the curve is steep, so rate is fast. As time goes on the curve flattens, so gradient gets smaller. That tells you rate is slowing down, finally reaching zero when the line is horizontal and reaction stops.
Final answer: The gradient decreases as reaction proceeds, showing the rate decreases until gradient is zero when reaction stops.

hints: Write the equation as Y + 2H2 gives C6H14 and note that Y has two C=C bonds, so decide which bonds are broken and which are made, ignoring bonds unchanged.
Recall the expression enthalpy change = energy to break bonds minus energy to make bonds, using Table 3.1 values.
walkthrough:
Write the bond changes simply**
Y is a $\text{C}_6$ diene, so $\text{Y} + 2\text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$. You do not need to count every $\text{C}-\text{H}$ and $\text{C}-\text{C}$. Cancel those that stay the same. Net change is: break $2 \times \text{C}=\text{C}$ and $2 \times \text{H}-\text{H}$, make $2 \times \text{C}-\text{C}$ and $4 \times \text{C}-\text{H}$.

Substitute and calculate**
Energy broken $$= (2 \times 610) + (2 \times 436) = 1220 + 872 = 2092 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$. Energy made $$= (4 \times 410) + (2 \times 350) = 1640 + 700 = 2340 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$. Then $$\Delta H = 2092 - 2340 = -248 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$. The negative sign shows the hydrogenation is exothermic, as expected when pi bonds are replaced by stronger sigma bonds.

Final answer: $$\Delta H = \Sigma(\text{bonds broken}) - \Sigma(\text{bonds made})$$
$$= [(2 \times 610) + (2 \times 436)] - [(4 \times 410) + (2 \times 350)]$$
$$= 2092 - 2340 = -248 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Remember what a nickel catalyst does to the activation energy pathway without changing temperature or the shape of the distribution.
walkthrough:
Show the catalyst effect**
Nickel is a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrogenation. It provides an alternative route of lower activation energy. On Fig. 3.3 you keep the distribution curve exactly the same because temperature T is unchanged, but you draw a new dashed $E_A$ line shifted to the left, at lower energy, to show the reduced barrier.
Final answer: New $E_A$ line drawn to the left of the original $E_A$ on the energy axis, with same curve shape.

hints: Compare the area beyond the new lower Ea with the original shaded area A to decide if B is larger or smaller.
Link a larger fraction of molecules with E >= Ea to collision frequency and rate, remembering that only energetic collisions with correct orientation succeed.
walkthrough:
Compare the areas**
Lowering $E_A$ moves the cut off to the left, so more of the tail of the distribution is included. Area B, the number of molecules with energy greater than or equal to the catalysed $E_A$, is therefore larger than area A.

Explain the rate effect through collisions**
For reaction, $\text{H}_2$ molecules must collide with sufficient energy to overcome $E_A$ and with correct orientation. With a bigger fraction able to clear the lower barrier, the frequency of effective, successful collisions per second rises, so the hydrogenation rate increases at the same temperature T.

Final answer: Area B is larger than area A, so rate of hydrogenation increases.
This is because a greater proportion of molecules have energy >= $E_A$, increasing the frequency of successful, effective collisions.

hints: Work backwards from the cleavage products, noting that (CH3)2C=O comes from a (CH3)2C= end and CO2 comes from a =CH2 end.
Remember that the three carbon diacid HOOCCH2COOH must come from a central =CH-CH2-CH= fragment joining the two double bonds.
walkthrough:
Assign each product to a fragment**
Hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves each $\text{C}=\text{C}$ completely. $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ can only come from $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=$, so one end of Z is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=$. $\text{CO}_2$ plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ comes from $\text{H}_2\text{C}=$, so the other end is $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}-$.

Join through the middle**
The remaining product $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH}$ has a $\text{CH}_2$ between two carboxyl carbons. That fits a central $-\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}-$ unit from two double bonds: $=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=$. Putting the ends together gives $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, which is 5-methylhexa-1,4-diene. Cleavage then gives exactly the four listed products.
Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2$
